clue.text: Tidal stream in Yorkshire ?

parts.note: tidal water is salt water, the sea's
a burn is a Scottish and northern word for a stream

explanation.surface: A clue asking which tidal stream runs through Yorkshire.
explanation.walkthrough: SALTBURN (Saltburn-by-the-Sea) is a seaside town on the Yorkshire coast; the question mark warns that the definition is only a location.
explanation.definitionFit: The answer names a resort town on the North Yorkshire coast, so it is a place found in that county.

clue.text: Bandage the governor after a sharp blow

parts.note: to swat is to strike with a quick sharp blow
HE is His Excellency, the title of a colonial governor

explanation.surface: Someone bandages the governor after he has been struck.
explanation.walkthrough: HE, for His Excellency, is the style of an ambassador or governor.
explanation.definitionFit: To swathe is to wrap round with cloth, as one binds a wound.

clue.text: Threw light on problem arising in the lab.

parts.note: lit means illuminated, threw light on

indicators.note: in a down clue arising means the word reads upwards, back to front

parts.note: a sum is an arithmetic problem

explanation.surface: Someone shed light on a difficulty that came up in the laboratory.
explanation.walkthrough: 'arising' turns SUM into MUS, read up the grid.
explanation.definitionFit: Litmus paper is a standard acid-alkali indicator used in chemistry laboratories.

clue.text: Scholars can take trouble, but get punishment

parts.note: BAs are Bachelors of Arts, graduates or scholars
a tin is a can
ado means fuss or trouble

explanation.surface: Students who make trouble end up being punished.
explanation.definitionFit: The bastinado is a beating on the soles of the feet, an old corporal punishment.

clue.text: Novel form of attic ?

explanation.surface: A fresh shape for a loft.
explanation.walkthrough: The first sense is John Braine's 1957 novel; the second describes a garret literally.
explanation.definitionFit: It is the title of John Braine's book, and a garret is literally the chamber up in the roof of a house.

clue.text: He's crazy to do the twist in a mac

indicators.note: dancing the twist suggests the letters of the following words writhing into a new order

explanation.surface: A man wearing a raincoat is mad to dance the twist.
explanation.definitionFit: A maniac is a madman, someone who is crazy.

clue.text: Sounds like an African love affair

indicators.note: says the answer is pronounced like the words that follow

parts.note: a Moor is a North African, so 'a Moor' is an African

explanation.surface: Something reminiscent of a romance in Africa.
explanation.walkthrough: Said aloud, 'a Moor' gives the French-derived word for a love affair.
explanation.definitionFit: An amour is a romance, often a secret or illicit one.

clue.text: Drove mischievous child to point up' valley

parts.note: an imp is a mischievous child
E, east, is a point of the compass

indicators.note: in a down clue up means the word reads backwards, upwards

parts.note: a dell is a small wooded valley

explanation.surface: Someone drove a naughty child up to a spot along the valley.
explanation.walkthrough: 'up' turns DELL into LLED; the stray apostrophe is a printing mark.
explanation.definitionFit: Impelled means forced or urged forward, as one drives cattle.

clue.text: Wood holds up everyone, having breakdown

indicators.note: the wood's letters hold the other piece inside them

parts.note: a copse is a small wood

indicators.note: in a down clue up means this word reads from bottom to top

parts.note: all means everyone

explanation.surface: A wood keeps everybody waiting, as they suffer a breakdown.
explanation.walkthrough: 'up' turns ALL into LLA, which 'holds' places inside COPSE.
explanation.definitionFit: A collapse is a sudden failure, physical or mental.

clue.text: Match 'must be put in a high place, he affirms

indicators.note: says the match goes inside the word for the high place

parts.note: a tor is a rocky hill or high place
a Test is an international cricket match

explanation.surface: A man insists that a match must be played somewhere lofty.
explanation.walkthrough: TEST goes in after the first letter of TOR, giving TTESTOR after A.
explanation.definitionFit: An attestor is one who bears witness, someone who affirms that something is true.

clue.text: Perhaps Mark is the sole G.P. to be replaced

indicators.note: the letters are to be put back in another order

parts.note: GP is a general practitioner, a family doctor

explanation.surface: Mark is the only family doctor and must be replaced.
explanation.walkthrough: Mark here is the evangelist, not a man's name or a score.
explanation.definitionFit: St Mark's account of Christ's life is one of the four books of the New Testament that tell it.

clue.text: Wonder if Tom has tennis arranged?

indicators.note: set in order differently, so the letters of these three words are rearranged

explanation.surface: Would it be amazing if Tom had tennis organised?
explanation.definitionFit: Astonishment is great surprise, the state of wonder.

clue.text: The time I met a nymph

parts.note: an hour is a unit of time

explanation.surface: When I met a nymph.
explanation.definitionFit: A houri is a beautiful maiden of the Muslim paradise, a nymph.

clue.text: A number in one country or another

indicators.note: says the A and the number go inside the first country

parts.note: Austria is a country of central Europe
L is the Roman numeral for fifty

explanation.surface: Someone counts a figure in one nation or the other.
explanation.walkthrough: AL goes inside AUSTRIA, after AUSTR.
explanation.definitionFit: The definition stands for a second nation, distinct from the first one named.

clue.text: Gateshead scientists meet epicures

parts.note: read as Gate's head, the first letter of gate
astronomers are scientists who study the stars

explanation.surface: Star-gazers from a town in north-east England meet some gourmets.
explanation.walkthrough: Gateshead is a town on the Tyne; split as 'Gate's head' it gives G.
explanation.definitionFit: Gastronomers are connoisseurs of good food, which is what epicures are.

clue.text: What the have-nots have not

parts.note: the poor are those without property, so what they lack is the holding of possessions

explanation.definitionFit: The have-nots are those with no possessions, so they lack any title to property.

clue.text: Shredded taro long used as poison

indicators.note: cut into pieces, so the letters of taro are torn up and rearranged

parts.note: to pine is to long for

explanation.surface: Grated taro has long been used to poison people.
explanation.definitionFit: Atropine is a toxic alkaloid from deadly nightshade.

clue.text: Blemish-boils, perhaps ?

explanation.surface: A spot on the skin, a boil.
explanation.walkthrough: Heat spots are small skin eruptions; read again, boils are heats, and a pot is what boils.
explanation.definitionFit: A heat spot is a red mark on the skin, and boils are an instance of such eruptions.

clue.text: Funny men have been booked

explanation.surface: Some comics have been hired for a show.
explanation.walkthrough: The second sense is literal: Graham Greene put them in a book, his 1966 novel of that name.
explanation.definitionFit: Comics are funny men, and Greene's novel of 1966 put such people between covers.

clue.text: Does as substitute for port

indicators.note: an alternative arrangement, so the letters of these words are switched round

explanation.surface: Someone acts as a stand-in for the port.
explanation.definitionFit: Odessa is a major Black Sea port in Ukraine.

clue.text: Though not in demand, it's often in request

definitions.text: Though not in demand, it's often in request

parts.words: Though not in demand, it's often in request
parts.note: a polite word added to a request but left out of an order

explanation.definitionFit: The courtesy word is used when asking politely and omitted when giving a command.

clue.text: Barbarian makes very big attempt to break faith

parts.note: OS stands for outsize, very big

indicators.note: the attempt splits the word for faith open

parts.note: troth is faith or a pledge of loyalty
a go is an attempt

explanation.surface: A savage makes a huge effort to break his word.
explanation.walkthrough: GO goes inside TROTH, after TRO.
explanation.definitionFit: The Ostrogoths were an eastern Gothic people who overran Italy, barbarians to the Romans.

clue.text: Bird found by river — large head

parts.note: the Ouse is a river in Yorkshire and another in East Anglia

indicators.note: the head of the word is its first letter

explanation.surface: A bird is found beside the river, with a big head.
explanation.definitionFit: The ousel is an old name for the blackbird, also used for the ring ousel and water ousel.

clue.text: The lake school ?

parts.note: reads as a style of poetry, but means a lake in Cumbria that also names a school

explanation.definitionFit: Rydal Water is a lake in the Lake District, and Rydal is also the name of a school.

clue.text: I'm after the tax !

parts.note: post is Latin for after, as in post-war

explanation.surface: I'm chasing the tax!
explanation.definitionFit: An impost is a levy or duty charged by authority.

clue.text: Gamble heads will get broken in Wales

parts.note: a bet is a gamble

indicators.note: breaking up the word lets its letters be rearranged

explanation.surface: A wager that heads will be smashed in Wales.
explanation.walkthrough: HEADS rearranges to HESDA. BETHESDA is a slate-quarrying town in North Wales.
explanation.definitionFit: The answer names a town in Gwynedd, so it is a place found in that country.

clue.text: Praises former lots of mince

parts.note: ex means former, as in ex-wife

indicators.note: to mince is to chop finely, so the word lots is chopped and rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone praises what used to be a lot of minced meat.
explanation.definitionFit: To extol is to speak highly of, to praise.

clue.text: Arrest bookmaker for causing obstruction

parts.note: to arrest is to stop
pages are what make up a book, so a page is a book-maker

explanation.surface: Police arrest a bookie for blocking the way.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bookmaker' reads as a turf accountant but means a page, one of the things a book is made of.
explanation.definitionFit: A stoppage is a blockage, something that halts flow.
